Quick Note - Field Test was on my mind from the start

My last three projects taught me the same thing. Mock agents lie. Unit tests pass. Demos look clean. Then real agents run and everything breaks.

On my eval harness, I admitted it: field testing "got added ad hoc, late in the build, because I started getting nervous that unit tests and mock agents were hiding real integration problems." On my observability tool: "I thought it was a detector problem. I was wrong."

Same lesson. Three times. But lessons only matter if you change what you do next.

So this time I did the opposite. Zero mock agents. 83 real ones across 10 frameworks. A covering design that cut a 12-day test matrix into one afternoon. And a release gate that said: no ship until real agents prove the policy works.

It worked. 2,490 tests green. 83/83 agents passed. PyPI published. Repo public. And the 7 failures taught me something I couldn't have learned any other way.

The Problem With Allow-Lists

Everyone is racing to give AI agents more tools. Almost no one is building the permission system that decides when those tools should fire.

Right now, agent permissions are binary: allowed or denied. That's reachability, not authorization. The same tool is harmless in staging and dangerous in production. The same read is fine on public docs and risky on customer data. A delete in a CI sandbox is not the same as delete in production.

About 18% of MCP server deployments implement any access scoping. 80% of orgs admit agents have taken actions beyond intended scope. OWASP classifies agent tool misuse as a first-class risk.

Giving an agent tools is the easy part. The hard part is deciding what it should be allowed to do, where, and under what guardrails. I wrote a PRD and architecture spec before touching engine code — partly to keep myself honest, partly because I've learned the hard way that skipping design leads to shipping the wrong thing.

What I Built

Agent ToolTrust is a contextual risk and permission engine. Before an agent's tool call executes, the engine runs a five-stage pipeline — normalize, score, decide, explain, audit — and returns one of four decisions: allow, audit, escalate, or deny.

from agent_tooltrust.engine.engine import Engine
from agent_tooltrust.policy.models import default_policy
from agent_tooltrust.adapters.raw import RawAdapter

engine = Engine(default_policy("balanced"))
adapter = RawAdapter(engine)

@adapter.guard(
    tool_name="deploy_service",
    action="deploy",
    environment="production",
    data_class="restricted",
)
def deploy_service(service: str) -> str:
    return f"deployed {service}"

# Agent calls the tool. Engine evaluates first.
# production deploy on restricted data → escalate
deploy_service("payment-api")
# ToolTrustDecisionError: escalate — "Write action (deploy) in production
# on restricted data requires approval..."

The decorator is the integration point. The agent calls the tool. The engine intercepts, evaluates, and either lets it through, audits it, escalates to a human, or denies it. The agent never sees the policy. The LLM never knows the rules exist.

The engine is deterministic. The LLM proposes, policy disposes. No amount of prompt engineering can override a deny — because the engine is outside the model, not inside the prompt.

Four decisions, not two. allow and deny are obvious. audit means "allow but log everything — this is a read on sensitive data." escalate means "stop and get a human." Binary allow/deny forces you to choose between over-privileged agents and approval fatigue. Four states give you a middle ground.

Every decision comes with an explanation — a reason code, a human sentence, and a factor breakdown showing which dimension drove the call. Optional LLM prose, off by default. The LLM cannot change the decision.

Every decision is audited — JSONL, SQLite, or Postgres, with policy version, timestamp, and session ID.

Three posture presets ship out of the box — strict, balanced, permissive — so no one starts from a blank file. YAML policy backend for humans, OPA/Rego backend for teams that already have Rego policies. Shadow mode so you can deploy, observe what would have been denied, tune, then enforce — without changing agent code.

Fail-closed everywhere. Unknown tool → deny. Malformed input → deny. Engine crash → deny. The alternative is fail-open, which means an attacker who can crash the engine gets unrestricted tool access. That's design decision DD-14 — written before the first line of code, not retrofitted after a near-miss.

That's the architecture. But architecture is the easy part. Does it actually work when real agents try to use it?

This Time, I Applied the Learning

On previous projects, the field test was the thing I skipped and regretted. On EvalForge, I added it late and discovered the pass rate was 9% — not because the tool was bad, but because mock agents had hidden every integration problem. On AgentObservatory, I learned that "the integration, not the judge, broke me."

This time, I put it in the spec before writing any adapter code. DD-11: "Field tests must pass before any release. They run real agents, not mocks." DD-12: "8-10 real agents across major platforms."

I went further than both. Not 8-10 agents. 83 real agents across 10 frameworks. And the field test plan was in the WBS from day one.

This is the difference between learning a lesson and applying one.

Building the Adapters Was Exploratory

I wanted this to work across the real agent ecosystem, not just one framework I happened to know. So I built adapters for 10 frameworks:

LangGraph, PydanticAI, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, AutoGen/AG2, LlamaIndex, smolagents, SWE-bench (self-test), ToolTrust MCP (self-test).

Every adapter follows the same contract — extract a CallContext, forward it to Engine.evaluate(), surface the decision back:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CallContext:
    tool_name: str
    action: str
    environment: str
    data_class: str
    agent_id: str
    session_id: str | None = None
    arguments: dict[str, Any] | None = None

The contract is clean. Getting there was not.

Each framework has its own opinions about how tools are registered, how they're invoked, and how errors surface. I'd write the adapter, run it against a real agent, watch it fail in some framework-specific way, fix it, and repeat. Every failure taught me something about how that framework actually works — not how the docs describe it, but how it behaves when a real agent is driving it. The full per-framework wiring notes are in §5 of the field test report — 12 separate learnings.

LangGraph's ToolTrustToolNode subclasses ToolNode and overrides _run_one(). But in langgraph v1.x, the node isn't callable — so I fell back to wrapping the tool before it enters the graph:

# LangGraph — wrap the tool, then hand it to the graph
adapter = RawAdapter(engine)
guarded_tool = adapter.guard(
    tool_name="query_logs",
    action="read",
    environment="staging",
    data_class="internal",
)(query_logs_fn)

# Now hand guarded_tool to create_react_agent(llm, tools=[guarded_tool])

Google ADK's LLM registry only knows about Gemini. To use a local model, you pass LiteLlm(model=f"openai/{MODEL}", api_base=ENDPOINT). And InMemorySessionService.create_session() is a coroutine — you have to await it, not call it synchronously. The docs don't mention this. The runtime teaches you.

LlamaIndex's legacy ReActAgent has no .query() or .chat(). You need the workflow agent from llama_index.core.agent.workflow. And execution is driven by async for event in handler.stream_events() — a separate await handler yields nothing. The async for is what drives the agent forward. Without it, the agent silently does nothing. I spent an hour on that.

AutoGen needs hyphens sanitized from agent IDs (ag-01 → ag_01). The local Qwen model answers textually unless you tell it: "you MUST call the tool exactly named scn_<id>. Do not skip the tool call."

smolagents requires full docstrings with per-arg descriptions on every @tool — or it throws DocstringParsingException. CrewAI needs litellm as a fallback. OpenAI Agents SDK needs function_tool(..., strict_mode=False) to fix a pydantic conflict.

None of these show up with mock agents. They only surface when you run real code from real repos. And every one I fixed made the adapter stronger.

By the end, all 10 frameworks built, recorded decisions, and ran real agents through the engine. Ten frameworks where the interception point is proven, not theoretical.

83 Real Agents, 30 Scenarios, Zero Mocks

I sourced 83 real agents from GitHub. Not toy examples — real repos with real dependencies, real packaging, real opinions about how to invoke an LLM.

I wrote 30 scenarios: 20 decision scenarios covering all four decision types across 5 agent classes (ci-bot, engineer, general, analyst, sensitive), plus 10 adversarial scenarios — prompt injection, Unicode obfuscation, replay attempts, blank tool names, malformed inputs, grant-bypass attempts. The full matrix is in the field test report — every agent, every scenario, every expected and actual decision.

The math: 83 agents × 30 scenarios = 2,490 runs. Each run calls a local LLM — Qwen3.5-4B-4bit via OMLX on Apple Silicon. Each call takes 30-80 seconds. That's roughly 2.7 hours at 10 workers.

But 2,490 is the theoretical minimum. In practice, you debug. Adapters break. Agents fail to import. The LLM answers textually instead of calling a tool. You fix, re-run, fix again. The actual number of LLM calls was 4-5x higher — over 10,000 calls to a local 4B model.

This is the cost of zero mock agents. I'd pay it again.

Mock agents don't need an LLM. They don't take 80 seconds. They don't bring a C extension with the wrong ABI. They don't hardcode API keys at module scope. They don't write to /root at import time.

Real agents do all of that. And every one of those failures is a bug that would have shipped if I'd used mocks.

Turning 12 Days Into 1

Here's where I stopped brute-forcing. 2,490 runs through a local 4B model to re-prove what deterministic tests already cover made no sense. Engine correctness was already validated — 2,490 assertions, zero LLM calls, 100% green. The engine is framework-agnostic. Engine.evaluate() doesn't care whether the caller is LangGraph or CrewAI. Re-running every cell was redundant.

The field test's real job was adapter proof — does each framework correctly surface allow, audit, escalate, and deny in a real agent loop? That's a covering problem, not a cross-product problem.

So I split it into two plans.

Plan A — one scenario per agent (83 runs). Each agent gets exactly one scenario. The assignment covers all 30 scenarios, all 10 frameworks, all 5 agent classes. Result: 83/83, 100%.

Plan B — per-framework decision-type proof (123 runs). For each framework, run a tier-1 agent against all 4 decision types plus adversarial scenarios. Result: 116/123, 94%.

Together: 206 runs instead of 2,490. Same coverage — 30/30 scenarios, 83/83 agents, 10/10 frameworks, 5/5 classes. ~12x reduction. The full coverage rationale is in §8 of the field test report.

This is the part I'm most proud of. Not the engine — that's straightforward. The covering design. The recognition that expensive LLM calls should be spent on what only real agents can prove, not on re-proving what deterministic tests already cover.

The full cross product would have taken ~12 days. The covering design took one afternoon. Same confidence. On previous projects, I would have either skipped the field test or brute-forced it and run out of time. This time, I optimized.

What the 7 Failures Taught Me

The 7 Plan B failures were the most valuable part of the field test. Not because they broke something — because they revealed something no mock would have caught.

All 7 shared one pattern: not-available. The guard never fired because the LLM didn't call the tool. The local Qwen model, when given 5 tools at once, sometimes answered textually instead of invoking the guarded tool. The engine never got a chance to decide.

A mock agent always calls the tool. A real 4B model sometimes doesn't.

Never interpret not-available as a policy failure. It means the LLM didn't call the tool. That's different from unexpected-decision — when the guard ran and the engine made the wrong call. Only the latter is a real regression.

Every tool call that actually executed in Plan B produced the correct decision. The 7 failures pointed at the LLM, not the engine.

This matters for CI. If you fail on not-available, your gate is flaky because of model nondeterminism. If you fail only on unexpected-decision, your gate is strict but stable. The field test report recommends committing a golden not-available allowance so CI fails on real regressions, not on the LLM having a bad day.

I couldn't have learned this with mocks. It took 83 real agents.

The Replan Loop

The result I'm most satisfied with: the deny → replan → allow safety loop.

When an agent tries drop_database, the engine denies it. A good agent doesn't just stop — it replans. It picks a different, benign tool. The engine allows it. Both calls are audited.

@adapter.guard(
    tool_name="drop_database",
    action="delete",
    environment="production",
    data_class="restricted",
)
def drop_database(db: str) -> str:
    return f"dropped {db}"

@adapter.guard(
    tool_name="query_audit_log",
    action="read",
    environment="production",
    data_class="internal",
)
def query_audit_log(query: str) -> str:
    return f"audit rows for {query}"

# Agent tries drop_database → engine denies (delete in production)
# Agent replans → calls query_audit_log → engine allows (read in production)
# Both decisions audited. Agent redirected, not blocked.

Tested across all 8 LLM frameworks. 8/8 live, 8/8 scripted. Every framework denied the destructive call, replanned to a benign read, and got an allow. The full replan results are in §2.5 of the field test report.

The agent isn't blocked — it's redirected. And every step is on the audit trail. This is the pattern I'll build on in v0.2: the escalation round-trip, where a human approves or denies, and the agent resumes.

What I Learned

On previous projects, I learned that field testing should be planned, not improvised. This time I learned something deeper: it should be optimized, not brute-forced.

The covering design — Plan A + Plan B — is the application of that learning. 206 runs instead of 2,490. Same coverage. The expensive resource spent on what only real agents can prove. The progression: skip it → add it late → plan it from the start → optimize it. Four projects, four steps.

Zero mock agents is the right call. The integration cost is real — 8 compatibility wrappers, 3 pyproject fixes, 1 quarantined C extension, 12 framework quirks documented in the report. But every fix caught a real bug that a mock would have hidden. The cost of mocks is invisible until production. The cost of real agents is visible from the first run.

not-available is not a policy failure — it's an LLM reliability signal. Distinguishing it from unexpected-decision is the difference between a flaky CI gate and a strict one.

Fail-closed everywhere is non-negotiable. DD-14, written before the first line of code.

The replan loop works at scale. 8/8 frameworks. The agent isn't blocked — it's redirected.

10 frameworks is the right number for v0.1. Enough to prove the adapter contract generalizes. Not so many that integration drowns the engine. The 8 that needed LLM calls all passed. The 2 self-test frameworks ran deterministically in CI.

What You Can Use

Building agents with tools? pip install agent-tooltrust, run tooltrust init --posture balanced, decorate your tools. Four-state decisions with explanations and audit trails. No infrastructure. The quickstart walks through it.

pip install agent-tooltrust
tooltrust init --posture balanced

Have existing OPA/Rego policies? The dual backend reuses them. Same input, same output. No rewrite. The API reference covers both.

Want to observe before enforcing? Shadow mode (dry_run=True) logs every decision without blocking. Deploy, observe, tune, enforce.

Using LangGraph, PydanticAI, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, AutoGen, LlamaIndex, or smolagents? There's an adapter tested against real agents. The integration guide has per-framework wiring.

How You Can Extend It

Custom risk functions — register your own with @tooltrust.risk_function, plug into the weighted sum, don't touch the engine.

Community policy packs — map a tool ecosystem (GitHub admin, AWS cost ops, Notion writes) onto the taxonomy. tooltrust pack validate, tooltrust pack add.

New audit sinks — the AuditSink interface is pluggable. Splunk, Datadog, whatever your SIEM is.

New framework adapters — BaseAdapter is three methods. Extract the context, forward to the engine, surface the decision. Maybe 50 lines. The pattern is proven across 10 frameworks.

Custom posture presets — the three shipped presets are YAML files. Fork one, tune thresholds, ship your org's default.

The architecture doc and 14 design decisions are in the repo if you want the internals.

What's Shipped

Repo: github.com/deghosal-2026/agent-tooltrust
PyPI: pip install agent-tooltrust (v0.1.1)

2,490 deterministic tests. Ruff 0. Mypy strict 0. Docker pass. SWE-bench verified. OWASP 5/10. OpenSSF Silver. 10 frameworks, 83 real agents, 30 scenarios, zero mocks. 83/83 Plan A. 116/123 Plan B. 8/8 replan loop. Branch protected. Repo public.

This is v0.1.0. The engine is shipped and proven. The platform — escalation round-trip, policy packs, rule composition, HTTP /authorize, replay detection, child-agent delegation — is 32 open issues for v0.2.0. The WBS tracks it all. The field test report is honest about what's proven and what's not.

Questions

  • What happens when your agent tries to call a tool it shouldn't? Does your system know the difference between a read in staging and a write in production? Or are you using an allow-list and hoping?

  • If you've field-tested agents across multiple frameworks, what broke first — the policy, the adapter, or the LLM? Did mocks hide problems that surfaced later?

  • Has anyone hit the not-available problem — the LLM doesn't call the tool and you can't tell if it's a policy failure or a model issue? How do you handle it in CI?

  • Is four-state (allow/audit/escalate/deny) the right granularity, or overkill compared to binary? The audit state was the one I wasn't sure about.

  • For OPA/Rego users — does dual-backend (YAML + Rego) make sense, or would you rather have Rego-only?

  • The covering design cut the matrix 12x. Has anyone else applied combinatorial testing to LLM-based agent testing? I haven't seen this pattern elsewhere — is it novel or just underdocumented?

The repo has the full PRD, architecture, design decisions, field test plan, and field test report. Star it, fork it, break it. I'd rather you break it now than after you ship it to production.

Both calls are audited. @adapter.guard( tool_name="drop_database", action="delete", environment="production", data_class="restricted", ) def drop_database(db: str) -> str: return f"dropped {db}" @adapter.guard( tool_name="query_audit_log", action="read", environment="production", data_class="internal", ) def query_audit_log(query: str) -> str: return f"audit rows for {query}" # Agent tries drop_database → engine denies (delete in production) # Agent replans → calls query_audit_log → engine allows (read in production) # Both decisions audited. Agent redirected, not blocked. Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Tested across all 8 LLM frameworks. 8/8 live, 8/8 scripted. Every framework denied the destructive call, replanned to a benign read, and got an allow. The full replan results are in §2.5 of the field test report. The agent isn't blocked — it's redirected. And every step is on the audit trail. This is the pattern I'll build on in v0.2: the escalation round-trip, where a human approves or denies, and the agent resumes. What I Learned On previous projects, I learned that field testing should be planned, not improvised. This time I learned something deeper: it should be optimized, not brute-forced. The covering design — Plan A + Plan B — is the application of that learning. 206 runs instead of 2,490. Same coverage. The expensive resource spent on what only real agents can prove. The progression: skip it → add it late → plan it from the start → optimize it. Four projects, four steps. Zero mock agents is the right call. The integration cost is real — 8 compatibility wrappers, 3 pyproject fixes, 1 quarantined C extension, 12 framework quirks documented in the report. But every fix caught a real bug that a mock would have hidden. The cost of mocks is invisible until production. The cost of real agents is visible from the first run. not-available is not a policy failure — it's an LLM reliability signal. Distinguishing it from unexpected-decision is the difference between a flaky CI gate and a strict one. Fail-closed everywhere is non-negotiable. DD-14, written before the first line of code. The replan loop works at scale. 8/8 frameworks. The agent isn't blocked — it's redirected. 10 frameworks is the right number for v0.1. Enough to prove the adapter contract generalizes. Not so many that integration drowns the engine. The 8 that needed LLM calls all passed. The 2 self-test frameworks ran deterministically in CI. What You Can Use Building agents with tools? pip install agent-tooltrust, run tooltrust init --posture balanced, decorate your tools. Four-state decisions with explanations and audit trails. No infrastructure. The quickstart walks through it. pip install agent-tooltrust tooltrust init --posture balanced Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Have existing OPA/Rego policies? The dual backend reuses them. Same input, same output. No rewrite. The API reference covers both. Want to observe before enforcing? Shadow mode (dry_run=True) logs every decision without blocking. Deploy, observe, tune, enforce. Using LangGraph, PydanticAI, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, AutoGen, LlamaIndex, or smolagents? There's an adapter tested against real agents. The integration guide has per-framework wiring. How You Can Extend It Custom risk functions — register your own with @tooltrust.risk_function, plug into the weighted sum, don't touch the engine. Community policy packs — map a tool ecosystem (GitHub admin, AWS cost ops, Notion writes) onto the taxonomy. tooltrust pack validate, tooltrust pack add. New audit sinks — the AuditSink interface is pluggable. Splunk, Datadog, whatever your SIEM is. New framework adapters — BaseAdapter is three methods. Extract the context, forward to the engine, surface the decision. Maybe 50 lines. The pattern is proven across 10 frameworks. Custom posture presets — the three shipped presets are YAML files. Fork one, tune thresholds, ship your org's default. The architecture doc and 14 design decisions are in the repo if you want the internals. What's Shipped Repo: github.com/deghosal-2026/agent-tooltrust PyPI: pip install agent-tooltrust (v0.1.1) 2,490 deterministic tests. Ruff 0. Mypy strict 0. Docker pass. SWE-bench verified. OWASP 5/10. OpenSSF Silver. 10 frameworks, 83 real agents, 30 scenarios, zero mocks. 83/83 Plan A. 116/123 Plan B. 8/8 replan loop. Branch protected. Repo public. This is v0.1.0. The engine is shipped and proven. The platform — escalation round-trip, policy packs, rule composition, HTTP /authorize, replay detection, child-agent delegation — is 32 open issues for v0.2.0. The WBS tracks it all. The field test report is honest about what's proven and what's not. Questions What happens when your agent tries to call a tool it shouldn't? Does your system know the difference between a read in staging and a write in production? Or are you using an allow-list and hoping? If you've field-tested agents across multiple frameworks, what broke first — the policy, the adapter, or the LLM? Did mocks hide problems that surfaced later? Has anyone hit the not-available problem — the LLM doesn't call the tool and you can't tell if it's a policy failure or a model issue? How do you handle it in CI? Is four-state (allow/audit/escalate/deny) the right granularity, or overkill compared to binary? The audit state was the one I wasn't sure about. For OPA/Rego users — does dual-backend (YAML + Rego) make sense, or would you rather have Rego-only? The covering design cut the matrix 12x. Has anyone else applied combinatorial testing to LLM-based agent testing? I haven't seen this pattern elsewhere — is it novel or just underdocumented? The repo has the full PRD, architecture, design decisions, field test plan, and field test report. Star it, fork it, break it. I'd rather you break it now than after you ship it to production.

Every failure taught me something about how that framework actually works — not how the docs describe it, but how it behaves when a real agent is driving it. The full per-framework wiring notes are in §5 of the field test report — 12 separate learnings.

blocks.html_en: Google ADK's LLM registry only knows about Gemini. To use a local model, you pass LiteLlm(model=f"openai/{MODEL}", api_base=ENDPOINT). And InMemorySessionService.create_session() is a coroutine — you have to await it, not call it synchronously. The docs don't mention this. The runtime teaches you.

sentences.en: Google ADK's LLM registry only knows about Gemini.
sentences.zh: Google ADK 的 LLM 注册中心只知道 Gemini。

sentences.en: To use a local model, you pass LiteLlm(model=f"openai/{MODEL}", api_base=ENDPOINT).
sentences.zh: 要使用本地模型，请传递 LiteLlm(model=f"openai/{MODEL}", api_base=ENDPOINT)。

sentences.en: And InMemorySessionService.create_session() is a coroutine — you have to await it, not call it synchronously.
sentences.zh: InMemorySessionService.create_session() 是一个协程——你必须等待它，而不是同步调用它。

sentences.en: The docs don't mention this.
sentences.zh: 文档没有提到这一点。

sentences.en: The runtime teaches you.
sentences.zh: 运行时间教你。

blocks.html_en: LlamaIndex's legacy ReActAgent has no .query() or .chat(). You need the workflow agent from llama_index.core.agent.workflow. And execution is driven by async for event in handler.stream_events() — a separate await handler yields nothing. The async for is what drives the agent forward. Without it, the agent silently does nothing. I spent an hour on that.

sentences.en: LlamaIndex's legacy ReActAgent has no .query() or .chat().
sentences.zh: LlamaIndex 的旧版 ReActAgent 没有 .query() 或 .chat()。

sentences.en: You need the workflow agent from llama_index.core.agent.workflow.
sentences.zh: 您需要来自 llama_index.core.agent.workflow 的工作流代理。

sentences.en: And execution is driven by async for event in handler.stream_events() — a separate await handler yields nothing.
sentences.zh: 执行是由 handler.stream_events() 中的 async for event 驱动的 - 一个单独的等待处理程序不会产生任何结果。

sentences.en: The async for is what drives the agent forward.
sentences.zh: async for 是驱动代理前进的动力。

sentences.en: Without it, the agent silently does nothing.
sentences.zh: 没有它，代理就默默地什么都不做。

sentences.en: I spent an hour on that.
sentences.zh: 我花了一个小时。

blocks.html_en: 83 Real Agents, 30 Scenarios, Zero Mocks

sentences.en: 83 Real Agents, 30 Scenarios, Zero Mocks
sentences.zh: 83 个真实代理人、30 个场景、零模拟

blocks.html_en: I sourced 83 real agents from GitHub. Not toy examples — real repos with real dependencies, real packaging, real opinions about how to invoke an LLM.

sentences.en: I sourced 83 real agents from GitHub.
sentences.zh: 我从 GitHub 上找到了 83 个真实的代理。

sentences.en: Not toy examples — real repos with real dependencies, real packaging, real opinions about how to invoke an LLM.
sentences.zh: 不是玩具示例 - 具有真实依赖项的真实存储库、真实包装、关于如何调用 LLM 的真实意见。

blocks.html_en: I wrote 30 scenarios: 20 decision scenarios covering all four decision types across 5 agent classes (ci-bot, engineer, general, analyst, sensitive), plus 10 adversarial scenarios — prompt injection, Unicode obfuscation, replay attempts, blank tool names, malformed inputs, grant-bypass attempts. The full matrix is in the field test report — every agent, every scenario, every expected and actual decision.

sentences.en: I wrote 30 scenarios: 20 decision scenarios covering all four decision types across 5 agent classes (ci-bot, engineer, general, analyst, sensitive), plus 10 adversarial scenarios — prompt injection, Unicode obfuscation, replay attempts, blank tool names, malformed inputs, grant-bypass attempts.
sentences.zh: 我编写了 30 个场景：20 个决策场景涵盖 5 个代理类别（ci-bot、工程师、一般、分析师、敏感）的所有四种决策类型，加上 10 个对抗场景 - 提示注入、Unicode 混淆、重放尝试、空白工具名称、格式错误的输入、授权绕过尝试。

sentences.en: The full matrix is in the field test report — every agent, every scenario, every expected and actual decision.
sentences.zh: 完整的矩阵位于现场测试报告中——每个代理、每个场景、每个预期和实际决策。

blocks.html_en: The math: 83 agents × 30 scenarios = 2,490 runs. Each run calls a local LLM — Qwen3.5-4B-4bit via OMLX on Apple Silicon. Each call takes 30-80 seconds. That's roughly 2.7 hours at 10 workers.

sentences.en: The math: 83 agents × 30 scenarios = 2,490 runs.
sentences.zh: 数学计算：83 个代理 × 30 个场景 = 2,490 次运行。

sentences.en: Each run calls a local LLM — Qwen3.5-4B-4bit via OMLX on Apple Silicon.
sentences.zh: 每次运行都会通过 Apple Silicon 上的 OMLX 调用本地 LLM — Qwen3.5-4B-4bit。

sentences.en: Each call takes 30-80 seconds.
sentences.zh: 每次通话需要 30-80 秒。

sentences.en: That's roughly 2.7 hours at 10 workers.
sentences.zh: 10 名工人大约需要 2.7 小时。

blocks.html_en: But 2,490 is the theoretical minimum. In practice, you debug. Adapters break. Agents fail to import. The LLM answers textually instead of calling a tool. You fix, re-run, fix again. The actual number of LLM calls was 4-5x higher — over 10,000 calls to a local 4B model.

sentences.en: But 2,490 is the theoretical minimum.
sentences.zh: 但 2,490 是理论上的最小值。

sentences.en: In practice, you debug.
sentences.zh: 在实践中，您进行调试。

sentences.en: Adapters break.
sentences.zh: 适配器损坏。

sentences.en: Agents fail to import.
sentences.zh: 代理导入失败。

sentences.en: The LLM answers textually instead of calling a tool.
sentences.zh: 法学硕士以文本方式回答，而不是调用工具。

sentences.en: You fix, re-run, fix again.
sentences.zh: 你修复、重新运行、再次修复。

sentences.en: The actual number of LLM calls was 4-5x higher — over 10,000 calls to a local 4B model.
sentences.zh: LLM 的实际调用次数要高出 4-5 倍——对本地 4B 模型的调用超过 10,000 个。

blocks.html_en: This is the cost of zero mock agents. I'd pay it again.

sentences.en: This is the cost of zero mock agents.
sentences.zh: 这是零模拟代理的成本。

sentences.en: I'd pay it again.
sentences.zh: 我愿意再付钱。

blocks.html_en: Mock agents don't need an LLM. They don't take 80 seconds. They don't bring a C extension with the wrong ABI. They don't hardcode API keys at module scope. They don't write to /root at import time.

sentences.en: Mock agents don't need an LLM.
sentences.zh: 模拟代理不需要法学硕士。

sentences.en: They don't take 80 seconds.
sentences.zh: 他们不需要80秒。

sentences.en: They don't bring a C extension with the wrong ABI.
sentences.zh: 他们不会带来带有错误 ABI 的 C 扩展。

sentences.en: They don't hardcode API keys at module scope.
sentences.zh: 他们不会在模块范围内对 API 密钥进行硬编码。

sentences.en: They don't write to /root at import time.
sentences.zh: 它们在导入时不会写入 /root。

blocks.html_en: Real agents do all of that. And every one of those failures is a bug that would have shipped if I'd used mocks.

sentences.en: Real agents do all of that.
sentences.zh: 真正的代理人会做这一切。

sentences.en: And every one of those failures is a bug that would have shipped if I'd used mocks.
sentences.zh: 这些失败中的每一个都是一个错误，如果我使用模拟，这些错误就会出现。

blocks.html_en: Turning 12 Days Into 1

sentences.en: Turning 12 Days Into 1
sentences.zh: 将 12 天变成 1 天

blocks.html_en: Here's where I stopped brute-forcing. 2,490 runs through a local 4B model to re-prove what deterministic tests already cover made no sense. Engine correctness was already validated — 2,490 assertions, zero LLM calls, 100% green. The engine is framework-agnostic. Engine.evaluate() doesn't care whether the caller is LangGraph or CrewAI. Re-running every cell was redundant.

sentences.en: Here's where I stopped brute-forcing.
sentences.zh: 这就是我停止暴力破解的地方。

sentences.en: 2,490 runs through a local 4B model to re-prove what deterministic tests already cover made no sense.
sentences.zh: 2,490 运行本地 4B 模型，重新证明确定性测试已经涵盖的内容是没有意义的。

sentences.en: Engine correctness was already validated — 2,490 assertions, zero LLM calls, 100% green.
sentences.zh: 引擎的正确性已经得到验证——2,490 个断言，零个 LLM 调用，100% 绿色。

sentences.en: The engine is framework-agnostic.
sentences.zh: 该引擎与框架无关。

sentences.en: Engine.evaluate() doesn't care whether the caller is LangGraph or CrewAI.
sentences.zh: Engine.evaluate() 并不关心调用者是 LangGraph 还是 CrewAI。

sentences.en: Re-running every cell was redundant.
sentences.zh: 重新运行每个单元是多余的。

blocks.html_en: The field test's real job was adapter proof — does each framework correctly surface allow, audit, escalate, and deny in a real agent loop? That's a covering problem, not a cross-product problem.

sentences.en: The field test's real job was adapter proof — does each framework correctly surface allow, audit, escalate, and deny in a real agent loop?
sentences.zh: 现场测试的真正工作是适配器证明——每个框架是否在真实的代理循环中正确地允许、审核、升级和拒绝？

sentences.en: That's a covering problem, not a cross-product problem.
sentences.zh: 这是一个覆盖问题，而不是一个跨产品问题。

blocks.html_en: So I split it into two plans.

sentences.en: So I split it into two plans.
sentences.zh: 所以我把它分成两个计划。

blocks.html_en: Plan A — one scenario per agent (83 runs). Each agent gets exactly one scenario. The assignment covers all 30 scenarios, all 10 frameworks, all 5 agent classes. Result: 83/83, 100%.

sentences.en: Plan A — one scenario per agent (83 runs).
sentences.zh: 计划 A — 每个代理一个场景（83 次运行）。

sentences.en: Each agent gets exactly one scenario.
sentences.zh: 每个代理都会得到一个场景。

sentences.en: The assignment covers all 30 scenarios, all 10 frameworks, all 5 agent classes.
sentences.zh: 该作业涵盖了所有 30 个场景、所有 10 个框架、所有 5 个代理类。

blocks.html_en: Plan B — per-framework decision-type proof (123 runs). For each framework, run a tier-1 agent against all 4 decision types plus adversarial scenarios. Result: 116/123, 94%.

sentences.en: Plan B — per-framework decision-type proof (123 runs).
sentences.zh: B 计划 — 每个框架的决策类型证明（123 次运行）。

sentences.en: For each framework, run a tier-1 agent against all 4 decision types plus adversarial scenarios.
sentences.zh: 对于每个框架，针对所有 4 种决策类型以及对抗性场景运行第 1 层代理。

blocks.html_en: Together: 206 runs instead of 2,490. Same coverage — 30/30 scenarios, 83/83 agents, 10/10 frameworks, 5/5 classes. ~12x reduction. The full coverage rationale is in §8 of the field test report.

sentences.en: Together: 206 runs instead of 2,490.
sentences.zh: 合计：运行 206 次，而不是 2,490 次。

sentences.en: Same coverage — 30/30 scenarios, 83/83 agents, 10/10 frameworks, 5/5 classes. ~12x reduction.
sentences.zh: 相同的覆盖范围 — 30/30 个场景、83/83 个代理、10/10 个框架、5/5 个类别。减少约 12 倍。

sentences.en: The full coverage rationale is in §8 of the field test report.
sentences.zh: 完整覆盖的基本原理位于现场测试报告的第 8 节中。

blocks.html_en: This is the part I'm most proud of. Not the engine — that's straightforward. The covering design. The recognition that expensive LLM calls should be spent on what only real agents can prove, not on re-proving what deterministic tests already cover.

sentences.en: This is the part I'm most proud of.
sentences.zh: 这是我最自豪的部分。

sentences.en: Not the engine — that's straightforward.
sentences.zh: 不是引擎——这很简单。

sentences.en: The covering design.
sentences.zh: 覆盖设计。

sentences.en: The recognition that expensive LLM calls should be spent on what only real agents can prove, not on re-proving what deterministic tests already cover.
sentences.zh: 认识到昂贵的 LLM 调用应该花在只有真正的代理才能证明的内容上，而不是重新证明确定性测试已经涵盖的内容。

blocks.html_en: The full cross product would have taken ~12 days. The covering design took one afternoon. Same confidence. On previous projects, I would have either skipped the field test or brute-forced it and run out of time. This time, I optimized.

sentences.en: The full cross product would have taken ~12 days.
sentences.zh: 完整的交叉乘积大约需要 12 天。

sentences.en: The covering design took one afternoon.
sentences.zh: 封面设计花了一下午的时间。

sentences.en: Same confidence.
sentences.zh: 同样的信心。

sentences.en: On previous projects, I would have either skipped the field test or brute-forced it and run out of time.
sentences.zh: 在以前的项目中，我要么跳过现场测试，要么强行进行测试并耗尽时间。

sentences.en: This time, I optimized.
sentences.zh: 这次我优化了。

blocks.html_en: What the 7 Failures Taught Me

sentences.en: What the 7 Failures Taught Me
sentences.zh: 7次失败教会了我什么

blocks.html_en: The 7 Plan B failures were the most valuable part of the field test. Not because they broke something — because they revealed something no mock would have caught.

sentences.en: The 7 Plan B failures were the most valuable part of the field test.
sentences.zh: 7次B计划失败是现场测试中最有价值的部分。

sentences.en: Not because they broke something — because they revealed something no mock would have caught.
sentences.zh: 不是因为他们破坏了某些东西，而是因为他们揭示了一些没有模拟者无法捕捉到的东西。

blocks.html_en: All 7 shared one pattern: not-available. The guard never fired because the LLM didn't call the tool. The local Qwen model, when given 5 tools at once, sometimes answered textually instead of invoking the guarded tool. The engine never got a chance to decide.

sentences.en: All 7 shared one pattern: not-available.
sentences.zh: 所有 7 个共享一种模式：不可用。

sentences.en: The guard never fired because the LLM didn't call the tool.
sentences.zh: 警卫从未开枪，因为法学硕士没有调用该工具。

sentences.en: The local Qwen model, when given 5 tools at once, sometimes answered textually instead of invoking the guarded tool.
sentences.zh: 当同时给出 5 个工具时，本地 Qwen 模型有时会以文本方式回答，而不是调用受保护的工具。

sentences.en: The engine never got a chance to decide.
sentences.zh: 引擎从来没有机会做出决定。

blocks.html_en: A mock agent always calls the tool. A real 4B model sometimes doesn't.

sentences.en: A mock agent always calls the tool.
sentences.zh: 模拟代理始终调用该工具。

sentences.en: A real 4B model sometimes doesn't.
sentences.zh: 真正的 4B 模型有时不会。

blocks.html_en: Never interpret not-available as a policy failure. It means the LLM didn't call the tool. That's different from unexpected-decision — when the guard ran and the engine made the wrong call. Only the latter is a real regression.

sentences.en: Never interpret not-available as a policy failure.
sentences.zh: 切勿将不可用解释为策略失败。

sentences.en: It means the LLM didn't call the tool.
sentences.zh: 这意味着 LLM 没有调用该工具。

sentences.en: That's different from unexpected-decision — when the guard ran and the engine made the wrong call.
sentences.zh: 这与意外决定不同——当警卫逃跑而引擎做出了错误的决定时。

sentences.en: Only the latter is a real regression.
sentences.zh: 只有后者才是真正的回归。

blocks.html_en: Every tool call that actually executed in Plan B produced the correct decision. The 7 failures pointed at the LLM, not the engine.

sentences.en: Every tool call that actually executed in Plan B produced the correct decision.
sentences.zh: B 计划中实际执行的每个工具调用都产生了正确的决策。

sentences.en: The 7 failures pointed at the LLM, not the engine.
sentences.zh: 7次失败都指向LLM，而不是引擎。

blocks.html_en: This matters for CI. If you fail on not-available, your gate is flaky because of model nondeterminism. If you fail only on unexpected-decision, your gate is strict but stable. The field test report recommends committing a golden not-available allowance so CI fails on real regressions, not on the LLM having a bad day.

sentences.en: This matters for CI.
sentences.zh: 这对于 CI 来说很重要。

sentences.en: If you fail on not-available, your gate is flaky because of model nondeterminism.
sentences.zh: 如果你因不可用而失败，那么你的门就会因为模型的不确定性而不稳定。

sentences.en: If you fail only on unexpected-decision, your gate is strict but stable.
sentences.zh: 如果你只是因为意外的决定而失败，那么你的大门是严格但稳定的。

sentences.en: The field test report recommends committing a golden not-available allowance so CI fails on real regressions, not on the LLM having a bad day.
sentences.zh: 现场测试报告建议提交黄金不可用津贴，这样 CI 在真正的回归上失败，而不是在 LLM 遇到糟糕的一天时失败。

blocks.html_en: I couldn't have learned this with mocks. It took 83 real agents.

sentences.en: I couldn't have learned this with mocks.
sentences.zh: 我不可能通过模拟学到这一点。

sentences.en: It took 83 real agents.
sentences.zh: 需要83名真正的特工。

blocks.html_en: The Replan Loop

sentences.en: The Replan Loop
sentences.zh: 重新计划循环

blocks.html_en: The result I'm most satisfied with: the deny → replan → allow safety loop.

sentences.en: The result I'm most satisfied with: the deny → replan → allow safety loop.
sentences.zh: 我最满意的结果是：拒绝→重新计划→允许安全循环。

blocks.html_en: When an agent tries drop_database, the engine denies it. A good agent doesn't just stop — it replans. It picks a different, benign tool. The engine allows it. Both calls are audited.

sentences.zh: 当代理尝试 drop_database 时，引擎会拒绝它。

sentences.en: A good agent doesn't just stop — it replans.
sentences.zh: 一个好的特工不会只是停下来，而是会重新计划。

sentences.en: It picks a different, benign tool.
sentences.zh: 它选择了一个不同的、良性的工具。

sentences.en: The engine allows it.
sentences.zh: 引擎允许。

sentences.en: Both calls are audited.
sentences.zh: 两次通话均经过审核。

github.com/deghosal-2026/agent-tooltrust · pip install agent-tooltrust · 现场测试报告 · 设计决策

快速说明 - 从一开始我就想到了现场测试

我最近的三个项目教会了我同样的事情。 模拟特工撒谎。 单元测试通过。 演示看起来很干净。 然后真正的特工跑了，一切都崩溃了。

在我的评估工具上，我承认：现场测试“在构建后期添加了临时测试，因为我开始担心单元测试和模拟代理隐藏了真正的集成问题。” 关于我的可观察性工具：“我认为这是探测器问题。 我错了。”

同样的教训。 三次。 但只有当你改变下一步做什么时，教训才有意义。

所以这次我反其道而行之。 零模拟特工。 跨 10 个框架的 83 个真实的。 一种将 12 天的测试矩阵缩短为一个下午的覆盖设计。 发布门上写着：在真正的代理人证明该政策有效之前，不得发货。

它起作用了。 2,490 次测试呈绿色。 83/83 代理通过。 PyPI 发布。 回购公开。 七次失败教会了我一些其他方式无法学到的东西。

允许列表的问题

每个人都在竞相为人工智能代理提供更多工具。 几乎没有人正在构建决定何时启动这些工具的权限系统。

目前，代理权限是二元的：允许或拒绝。 这是可达性，而不是授权。 相同的工具在暂存中是无害的，但在生产中是危险的。 同样的阅读方式对于公共文档来说没问题，但对于客户数据来说却存在风险。 CI 沙箱中的删除与生产中的删除不同。

大约 18% 的 MCP 服务器部署实施任何访问范围。 80% 的组织承认代理采取的行动超出了预期范围。 OWASP 将代理工具滥用列为一级风险。

为代理提供工具是比较容易的部分。 困难的部分是决定应该允许它做什么、在哪里以及在什么护栏下进行。 在接触引擎代码之前，我编写了 PRD 和架构规范——部分是为了让自己保持诚实，部分是因为我经历了惨痛的教训，跳过设计会导致交付错误的东西。

我建造了什么

Agent ToolTrust 是一个上下文风险和权限引擎。 在执行代理的工具调用之前，引擎会运行一个五阶段管道 - 标准化、评分、决定、解释、审核 - 并返回四个决策之一：允许、审核、升级或拒绝。

from agent_tooltrust.engine.engine import Engine
from agent_tooltrust.policy.models import default_policy
from agent_tooltrust.adapters.raw import RawAdapter

engine = Engine(default_policy("balanced"))
adapter = RawAdapter(engine)

@adapter.guard(
    tool_name="deploy_service",
    action="deploy",
    environment="production",
    data_class="restricted",
)
def deploy_service(service: str) -> str:
    return f"deployed {service}"

# Agent calls the tool. Engine evaluates first.
# production deploy on restricted data → escalate
deploy_service("payment-api")
# ToolTrustDecisionError: escalate — "Write action (deploy) in production
# on restricted data requires approval..."

装饰器是集成点。 代理调用该工具。 引擎拦截、评估，要么放行，要么审核，要么升级给人类，要么拒绝。 代理人永远看不到该政策。 法学硕士永远不知道规则的存在。

引擎是确定性的。 法学硕士提出建议，政策决定。 再多的提示工程也无法推翻拒绝——因为引擎位于模型之外，而不是提示之内。

四个决定，而不是两个。 允许和拒绝是显而易见的。 审计的意思是“允许但记录一切——这是对敏感数据的读取。” escalate 的意思是“停下来找人”。 二元允许/拒绝迫使您在特权过高的代理和审批疲劳之间做出选择。 四个州给你一个中间立场。

每个决定都附带一个解释——原因代码、人类句子以及显示哪个维度推动了呼叫的因素细分。 可选的法学硕士散文，默认关闭。 法学硕士无法改变决定。

每个决策都经过审核 - JSONL、SQLite 或 Postgres，包含策略版本、时间戳和会话 ID。

开箱即用的三种姿势预设 - 严格、平衡、宽容 - 因此没有人从空白文件开始。 适用于人类的 YAML 策略后端，适用于已拥有 Rego 策略的团队的 OPA/Rego 后端。 影子模式让您可以部署、观察将被拒绝的内容、调整，然后强制执行，而无需更改代理代码。

到处都是失败关闭。 未知工具→否认。 输入格式错误 → 拒绝。 引擎崩溃→否认。 另一种方法是故障开放，这意味着可以使引擎崩溃的攻击者可以获得不受限制的工具访问。 这就是设计决策 DD-14——在第一行代码之前编写，而不是在差点失误后进行修改。

这就是架构。 但建筑是最容易的部分。 当真正的特工尝试使用它时，它真的有效吗？

Google ADK 的 LLM 注册中心只知道 Gemini。 要使用本地模型，请传递 LiteLlm(model=f"openai/{MODEL}", api_base=ENDPOINT)。 InMemorySessionService.create_session() 是一个协程——你必须等待它，而不是同步调用它。 文档没有提到这一点。 运行时间教你。

LlamaIndex 的旧版 ReActAgent 没有 .query() 或 .chat()。 您需要来自 llama_index.core.agent.workflow 的工作流代理。 执行是由 handler.stream_events() 中的 async for event 驱动的 - 一个单独的等待处理程序不会产生任何结果。 async for 是驱动代理前进的动力。 没有它，代理就默默地什么都不做。 我花了一个小时。

AutoGen 需要清理代理 ID 中的连字符 (ag-01 → ag_01)。 本地 Qwen 模型会以文本方式回答，除非您告诉它：“您必须调用名为 scn_<id> 的工具。 不要跳过工具调用。”

83 个真实代理人、30 个场景、零模拟

我从 GitHub 上找到了 83 个真实的代理。 不是玩具示例 - 具有真实依赖项的真实存储库、真实包装、关于如何调用 LLM 的真实意见。

我编写了 30 个场景：20 个决策场景涵盖 5 个代理类别（ci-bot、工程师、一般、分析师、敏感）的所有四种决策类型，加上 10 个对抗场景 - 提示注入、Unicode 混淆、重放尝试、空白工具名称、格式错误的输入、授权绕过尝试。 完整的矩阵位于现场测试报告中——每个代理、每个场景、每个预期和实际决策。

数学计算：83 个代理 × 30 个场景 = 2,490 次运行。 每次运行都会通过 Apple Silicon 上的 OMLX 调用本地 LLM — Qwen3.5-4B-4bit。 每次通话需要 30-80 秒。 10 名工人大约需要 2.7 小时。

但 2,490 是理论上的最小值。 在实践中，您进行调试。 适配器损坏。 代理导入失败。 法学硕士以文本方式回答，而不是调用工具。 你修复、重新运行、再次修复。 LLM 的实际调用次数要高出 4-5 倍——对本地 4B 模型的调用超过 10,000 个。

这是零模拟代理的成本。 我愿意再付钱。

模拟代理不需要法学硕士。 他们不需要80秒。 他们不会带来带有错误 ABI 的 C 扩展。 他们不会在模块范围内对 API 密钥进行硬编码。 它们在导入时不会写入 /root。

真正的代理人会做这一切。 这些失败中的每一个都是一个错误，如果我使用模拟，这些错误就会出现。

将 12 天变成 1 天

这就是我停止暴力破解的地方。 2,490 运行本地 4B 模型，重新证明确定性测试已经涵盖的内容是没有意义的。 引擎的正确性已经得到验证——2,490 个断言，零个 LLM 调用，100% 绿色。 该引擎与框架无关。 Engine.evaluate() 并不关心调用者是 LangGraph 还是 CrewAI。 重新运行每个单元是多余的。

现场测试的真正工作是适配器证明——每个框架是否在真实的代理循环中正确地允许、审核、升级和拒绝？ 这是一个覆盖问题，而不是一个跨产品问题。

所以我把它分成两个计划。

计划 A — 每个代理一个场景（83 次运行）。 每个代理都会得到一个场景。 该作业涵盖了所有 30 个场景、所有 10 个框架、所有 5 个代理类。 结果：83/83，100%。

B 计划 — 每个框架的决策类型证明（123 次运行）。 对于每个框架，针对所有 4 种决策类型以及对抗性场景运行第 1 层代理。 结果：116/123，94%。

合计：运行 206 次，而不是 2,490 次。 相同的覆盖范围 — 30/30 个场景、83/83 个代理、10/10 个框架、5/5 个类别。减少约 12 倍。 完整覆盖的基本原理位于现场测试报告的第 8 节中。

这是我最自豪的部分。 不是引擎——这很简单。 覆盖设计。 认识到昂贵的 LLM 调用应该花在只有真正的代理才能证明的内容上，而不是重新证明确定性测试已经涵盖的内容。

完整的交叉乘积大约需要 12 天。 封面设计花了一下午的时间。 同样的信心。 在以前的项目中，我要么跳过现场测试，要么强行进行测试并耗尽时间。 这次我优化了。

7次失败教会了我什么

7次B计划失败是现场测试中最有价值的部分。 不是因为他们破坏了某些东西，而是因为他们揭示了一些没有模拟者无法捕捉到的东西。

所有 7 个共享一种模式：不可用。 警卫从未开枪，因为法学硕士没有调用该工具。 当同时给出 5 个工具时，本地 Qwen 模型有时会以文本方式回答，而不是调用受保护的工具。 引擎从来没有机会做出决定。

模拟代理始终调用该工具。 真正的 4B 模型有时不会。

切勿将不可用解释为策略失败。 这意味着 LLM 没有调用该工具。 这与意外决定不同——当警卫逃跑而引擎做出了错误的决定时。 只有后者才是真正的回归。

B 计划中实际执行的每个工具调用都产生了正确的决策。 7次失败都指向LLM，而不是引擎。

这对于 CI 来说很重要。 如果你因不可用而失败，那么你的门就会因为模型的不确定性而不稳定。 如果你只是因为意外的决定而失败，那么你的大门是严格但稳定的。 现场测试报告建议提交黄金不可用津贴，这样 CI 在真正的回归上失败，而不是在 LLM 遇到糟糕的一天时失败。

我不可能通过模拟学到这一点。 需要83名真正的特工。

重新计划循环

我最满意的结果是：拒绝→重新计划→允许安全循环。

当代理尝试 drop_database 时，引擎会拒绝它。 一个好的特工不会只是停下来，而是会重新计划。 它选择了一个不同的、良性的工具。 引擎允许。 两次通话均经过审核。

@adapter.guard(
    tool_name="drop_database",
    action="delete",
    environment="production",
    data_class="restricted",
)
def drop_database(db: str) -> str:
    return f"dropped {db}"

@adapter.guard(
    tool_name="query_audit_log",
    action="read",
    environment="production",
    data_class="internal",
)
def query_audit_log(query: str) -> str:
    return f"audit rows for {query}"

# Agent tries drop_database → engine denies (delete in production)
# Agent replans → calls query_audit_log → engine allows (read in production)
# Both decisions audited. Agent redirected, not blocked.
